claim: Nucleosomes represent mechanical and energetic barriers that RNA Polymerase II (Pol II) must overcome during transcription.
source: Nucleosomes represent mechanical and energetic barriers that RNA Polymerase II (Pol II) must overcome during transcription.
evidence: This is a foundational statement in the abstract supported by established scientific knowledge about nucleosome function and the experimental work presented in the manuscript.

claim: Pol II crossing dynamics are complex, displaying pauses at specific loci, backtracking, and nucleosome hopping between wrapped states.
source: Pol II crossing dynamics are complex, displaying pauses at specific loci, backtracking, and nucleosome hopping between wrapped states.
evidence: This claim is supported by direct experimental observations from the single-molecule transcription assays shown in Figures 4-6.

claim: H2A.Z widens the nucleosome barrier.
source: While H2A.Z widens the barrier, uH2B heightens it, and both modifications greatly lengthen Pol II crossing time.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from both unzipping and transcription assays shown in Figures 1, 2, 6, and 7.

claim: uH2B heightens the nucleosome barrier.
source: While H2A.Z widens the barrier, uH2B heightens it, and both modifications greatly lengthen Pol II crossing time.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from both unzipping and transcription assays shown in Figures 1, 2, 6, and 7.

claim: Both H2A.Z and uH2B modifications greatly lengthen Pol II crossing time.
source: While H2A.Z widens the barrier, uH2B heightens it, and both modifications greatly lengthen Pol II crossing time.
evidence: This is directly measured and shown in Figure 6B and Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: The orthogonal barrier modifications of H2A.Z and uH2B rationalize their observed enrichment in +1 nucleosomes.
source: The orthogonal barrier modifications of H2A.Z and uH2B, and their effects on Pol II dynamics rationalize their observed enrichment in +1 nucleosomes and suggest a mechanism for selective control of gene expression.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data combined with cited literature about +1 nucleosome composition.

claim: In canonical nucleosomes, a core histone octamer made up of two copies of histones H2A, H2B, H3 and H4, is wrapped by ~147 basepairs (bp) of DNA.
source: In canonical (hereafter referred to as WT) nucleosomes, a core histone octamer made up of two copies of histones H2A, H2B, H3 and H4, is wrapped by ~147 basepairs (bp) of DNA.
evidence: This is established knowledge about nucleosome structure.

claim: Variations in DNA sequence, wrapping strength asymmetry, and position-dependent histone-DNA interactions are collectively responsible for the uneven character and polarity of the nucleosomal barrier to an elongating polymerase.
source: Variations in DNA sequence, wrapping strength asymmetry, and position-dependent histone-DNA interactions are collectively responsible for the uneven character and polarity of the nucleosomal barrier to an elongating polymerase (Bondarenko et al., 2006; Hall et al., 2009; Ngo et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Pol II has been shown to be capable of transcribing through the nucleosome both in vitro and in vivo.
source: Although Pol II has been shown to be capable of transcribing through the nucleosome both in vitro (Bondarenko et al., 2006) and in vivo (Weber et al., 2014), the detailed, high-resolution dynamics of Pol II crossing the nucleosomal barrier have not been observed yet.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The detailed, high-resolution dynamics of Pol II crossing the nucleosomal barrier have not been observed yet.
source: Although Pol II has been shown to be capable of transcribing through the nucleosome both in vitro (Bondarenko et al., 2006) and in vivo (Weber et al., 2014), the detailed, high-resolution dynamics of Pol II crossing the nucleosomal barrier have not been observed yet.
evidence: This statement establishes the gap in knowledge that the current study addresses.

claim: The majority of eukaryotic genes have a well-defined +1 nucleosome.
source: The majority of eukaryotic genes have a well-defined +1 nucleosome (the first nucleosome encountered by Pol II following initiation), which is enriched in H2A.Z and uH2B histones (Rhee et al., 2014; Teves et al., 2014), and represents the highest barrier to transcription (Teves et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous genomic studies.

claim: The +1 nucleosome is enriched in H2A.Z and uH2B histones.
source: The majority of eukaryotic genes have a well-defined +1 nucleosome (the first nucleosome encountered by Pol II following initiation), which is enriched in H2A.Z and uH2B histones (Rhee et al., 2014; Teves et al., 2014), and represents the highest barrier to transcription (Teves et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous genomic studies.

claim: The +1 nucleosome represents the highest barrier to transcription.
source: The majority of eukaryotic genes have a well-defined +1 nucleosome (the first nucleosome encountered by Pol II following initiation), which is enriched in H2A.Z and uH2B histones (Rhee et al., 2014; Teves et al., 2014), and represents the highest barrier to transcription (Teves et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Early optical tweezers studies have shown that in front of a WT nucleosome, Pol II slows down, pauses, backtracks, and cannot actively 'peel' the DNA wrapped around the histones.
source: Early optical tweezers studies have shown that in front of a WT nucleosome, Pol II slows down, pauses, backtracks, and cannot actively 'peel' the DNA wrapped around the histones (Hodges et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous optical tweezers work.

claim: The polymerase functions as a fluctuating ratchet that advances by rectifying transient, spontaneous wrapping/unwrapping transitions of the nucleosomal DNA around the histone core.
source: Instead, the polymerase functions as a fluctuating ratchet that advances by rectifying transient, spontaneous wrapping/unwrapping transitions of the nucleosomal DNA around the histone core (Hodges et al., 2009).
evidence: This is a mechanistic model supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Previous studies using tailless histones and mutated DNA sequences suggest that these nucleosomal elements modulate the topography of the barrier by affecting the density and duration of Pol II pauses.
source: A similar study using tailless histones and mutated DNA sequences suggests that these nucleosomal elements modulate the topography of the barrier by affecting the density and duration of Pol II pauses (Bintu et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Previous studies failed to accurately map the topography of the barrier and its effects on the dynamics of transcription because of their low resolution.
source: However, because of their low resolution, these studies failed to accurately map the topography of the barrier and its effects on the dynamics of transcription.
evidence: This is a critical assessment of previous work based on their methodological limitations.

claim: Prior attempts to characterize the nucleosomal barrier to transcription have suffered from two substantial limitations.
source: Prior attempts to characterize the nucleosomal barrier to transcription have suffered from two substantial limitations.
evidence: This statement introduces the limitations that the current study overcomes.

claim: Previous assessment of nucleosome stability relied on pulling and unwrapping the nucleosome from both ends.
source: First, previous assessment of nucleosome stability relied on pulling and unwrapping the nucleosome from both ends (Mihardja et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous methodology.

claim: Previous pulling experiments may not fully recapitulate the physical process of nucleosome invasion by Pol II, which unidirectionally unwinds the nucleosomal DNA.
source: These experiments, while providing a measure of the strength of DNA/histone interactions, may not fully recapitulate the physical process of nucleosome invasion by Pol II, which unidirectionally unwinds the nucleosomal DNA.
evidence: This is a critical assessment based on mechanistic reasoning.

claim: Transcription trajectories can now be obtained with millisecond temporal and near bp spatial resolution using optical tweezers.
source: Second, although we can now obtain transcription trajectories with millisecond temporal and near bp spatial resolution using optical tweezers (Righini et al., 2018), it is very difficult to determine the absolute location of the polymerase on the template (Hodges et al., 2009; Bintu et al., 2012; Fitz et al., 2016), what we term here 'accuracy'.
evidence: This is supported by citation to recent technical advances.

claim: It is very difficult to determine the absolute location of the polymerase on the template in previous optical tweezers experiments.
source: Second, although we can now obtain transcription trajectories with millisecond temporal and near bp spatial resolution using optical tweezers (Righini et al., 2018), it is very difficult to determine the absolute location of the polymerase on the template (Hodges et al., 2009; Bintu et al., 2012; Fitz et al., 2016), what we term here 'accuracy'.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work and identifies a key limitation.

claim: The study surmounts both limitations, obtaining high-resolution, high-accuracy topographic and transcriptional maps of WT and modified nucleosomes.
source: Here we surmount both limitations, obtaining high-resolution, high-accuracy topographic and transcriptional maps of WT and modified nucleosomes.
evidence: This is the main claim of the paper, supported by the experimental data presented throughout.

claim: The stem ahead of the fork consists of two consecutive segments of '601' nucleosome positioning sequence (NPS).
source: We engineered the stem ahead of the fork to consist of two consecutive segments of '601' nucleosome positioning sequence (NPS) (Lowary and Widom, 1998), and a short hairpin loop at the end to prevent tether breaking once all double-stranded DNA (dsDNA) is converted into single-stranded DNA (ssDNA) (Figure 1A).
evidence: This describes the experimental design shown in Figure 1A.

claim: When the force reaches ~17 pN, the dsDNA at the stem begins to unzip.
source: When the force reaches ~17 pN, the dsDNA at the stem begins to unzip.
evidence: This is an experimental observation from the unzipping assay.

claim: When the stem segment does not contain a nucleosome, the DNA unzips following a series of closely spaced transitions occurring in a narrow range of forces between 17–20 pN.
source: When the stem segment does not contain a nucleosome, the DNA unzips following a series of closely spaced transitions occurring in a narrow range of forces between 17–20 pN, dictated by the sequence of the template.
evidence: This is an experimental observation shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The highly reproducible force-extension signatures from the two consecutive NPS regions allow alignment of traces from different unzipping experiments.
source: The highly reproducible force-extension signatures from the two consecutive NPS regions allow us to align traces from different unzipping experiments by placing the force and dwell-time of the opening junction at each base pair into register (Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This describes the data analysis method supported by the reproducibility shown in the figures.

claim: Full DNA unzipping led to complete histone removal in ~75% of cases.
source: Relaxation of the tether results in two identical, sequential rezipping signatures characteristic of the naked DNA in ~75% of the cases (Figure 1B and C), indicating that full DNA unzipping led to complete histone removal.
evidence: This is a quantitative experimental observation from the unzipping assay.

claim: In 25% of cases, the second round of unzipping shows residual histone-DNA interactions from nucleosomal relics.
source: However, in 25% of the cases, when we unzip the same molecule for the second time, the force reaches higher values than with bare DNA but lower than those observed the first time, likely reflecting residual histone-DNA interactions from nucleosomal relics.
evidence: This is an experimental observation with an interpretation.

claim: The unzipping fork dwells in the WT nucleosome primarily at 25, 31, and 35 bp into the nucleosome in force-jump experiments at 28 pN.
source: In these experiments, the bare DNA construct unzips to the hairpin end instantaneously, while the fork dwells in the WT nucleosome primarily at 25, 31, and 35 bp into the nucleosome (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is an experimental observation from constant force unzipping shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The unzipping fork encounters substantial resistance at around 17, 26, 31, 41, 52, 61 and 69 bp into the nucleosome.
source: The topography maps reveal that the unzipping fork encounters substantial resistance at around 17, 26, 31, 41, 52, 61 and 69 bp into the nucleosome, which correspond to regions of proximal dimer and tetramer interaction with the first half of nucleosomal DNA (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is an experimental observation from the topography maps shown in Figure 1E.

claim: The resistance diminishes significantly after the dyad.
source: Interestingly, the resistance diminishes significantly after the dyad, suggesting that unzipping the first half of the nucleosome destabilizes the histone-DNA interactions of the second half.
evidence: This is an experimental observation with an interpretation.

claim: Major histone-DNA interactions first occur ~55 bp from the dyad and exhibit 5 or 10 bp periodicity.
source: As previously observed, major histone-DNA interactions first occur ~55 bp from the dyad and exhibit 5 or 10 bp periodicity as the unzipping fork progresses (Hall et al., 2009; Rudnizky et al., 2016).
evidence: This observation is consistent with previous work cited.

claim: The 5 or 10 bp periodicity probably reflects the strong histone-DNA contacts along the DNA minor groove every 10 bp observed in the crystal structure of the nucleosome.
source: This observation probably reflects the strong histone-DNA contacts along the DNA minor groove every 10 bp observed in the crystal structure of the nucleosome (Luger et al., 1997).
evidence: This is an interpretation based on structural knowledge from cited work.

claim: Unzipping of tetrasomes revealed a substantially diminished barrier compared to the octamer.
source: Unzipping of tetrasomes (H3/H4 tetramer assembled on NPS) revealed a substantially diminished barrier compared to the octamer, with unzipping fork dwelling events mostly restricted to locations near the dyad, and much lower maximum force reached during the unzipping process (Figure 1E, Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is an experimental observation from tetrasome unzipping shown in Figure 1E.

claim: The H2A/H2B dimer not only interacts locally with the DNA but also affects the strength of the H3/H4 tetramer-DNA interaction near the dyad.
source: These data indicate that the H2A/H2B dimer not only interacts locally with the DNA but it also affects the strength of the H3/H4 tetramer-DNA interaction near the dyad to orchestrate the overall nucleosome stability.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the tetrasome data.

claim: Loss or exchange of H2A/H2B dimers has been implicated in DNA replication, transcription, repair, and DNA supercoiling.
source: As loss or exchange of H2A/H2B dimers has been implicated in important biological processes such as DNA replication (Ramachandran and Henikoff, 2015), transcription (Ramachandran et al., 2017; Kireeva et al., 2002), repair (Ransom et al., 2010), and DNA supercoiling (Sheinin et al., 2013); these findings highlight the potential role of non-local histone-DNA interactions in those processes.
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: uH2B nucleosomes stabilize the dimer region (16 and 25 bp peaks) with minor effects on the tetramer region.
source: Specifically, uH2B nucleosomes stabilize the dimer region (16 and 25 bp peaks) with minor effects on the tetramer region (Figures 1E and 2B), suggesting that the attachment of ubiquitin to H2B enhances the barrier height locally.
evidence: This is an experimental observation from Figures 1E and 2B with an interpretation.

claim: H2A.Z nucleosomes show enhanced peaks at 41 and 52 bp, while exhibiting much lower heights at 25 and 31 bp.
source: H2A.Z nucleosomes show enhanced peaks at 41 and 52 bp, while exhibiting much lower heights at 25 and 31 bp (Figures 1E and 2B), indicating a global redistribution of the barrier's strength along its width.
evidence: This is an experimental observation from Figures 1E and 2B with an interpretation.

claim: In H2A.Z nucleosomes the dwell-time peaks are more broadly distributed throughout the first half of the barrier than in their WT or uH2B counterparts.
source: Overall, in H2A.Z nucleosomes the dwell-time peaks are more broadly distributed throughout the first half of the barrier than in their WT or uH2B counterparts, while maintaining their 5 to 10 bp periodicity.
evidence: This is an experimental observation from the topography maps.

claim: The H2A.Z-containing nucleosome has on average one more transition per trace than its WT counterpart.
source: Indeed, the H2A.Z-containing nucleosome has on average one more transition per trace than its WT counterpart (Figure 1—figure supplement 1F) but displays a similar standard deviation.
evidence: This is a quantitative experimental observation shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1F.

claim: No lateral mobility was observed with either WT or H2A.Z nucleosomes in partial unzipping-rezipping experiments.
source: Surprisingly, in contrast to the report by Rudnizky et al. (2016), we observed no lateral mobility with either WT or H2A.Z nucleosomes, as indicated by the highly reversible and overlapping unzipping signatures in the proximal dimer region (Figure 1—figure supplement 1G and H).
evidence: This is an experimental observation that contradicts previous work.

claim: The effect of the H2A.Z histone variant is not to increase the heterogeneity of the nucleosome population but to significantly redistribute the strength of the barrier.
source: Together, these results indicate that the effect of the H2A.Z histone variant in our experiments is not to increase the heterogeneity of the nucleosome population but to significantly redistribute the strength of the barrier, effectively broadening it.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on multiple experimental observations.

claim: The H2A.Z octamer is more stable than its WT counterpart within the nucleosome.
source: Like a previous study (Park et al., 2004), our data support the idea that the H2A.Z octamer is more stable than its WT counterpart within the nucleosome.
evidence: This is supported by the current data and a citation to previous work.

claim: Significantly less hexasome formation was consistently observed with H2A.Z than with H2A during nucleosome assembly.
source: As the ratio of octamer to DNA is increased during nucleosome reconstitution, we consistently observed significantly less hexasome formation with H2A.Z than with H2A (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is an experimental observation from assembly assays shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The M3 and M7 regions within H2A.Z are important for conferring increased octamer stability.
source: We found that this DNA configuration is more prone to hexasome formation due to the asymmetric nature of the 601 sequence. Two octamer-to-DNA ratios are tested for each sample and are shown below its corresponding lanes. The nucleosome, hexasome or DNA bands are indicated on the right. (B) Sequence alignment of H2A and H2A.Z swap mutants. Nomenclature of the swap mutants follows Clarkson et al. (1999).
evidence: This is based on experiments with swap mutants shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The M3 region corresponds to the 'loop 1' that mediates H2A.Z-H2A.Z interactions within the octamer.
source: Structurally the M3 region corresponds to the 'loop 1' that mediates H2A.Z-H2A.Z interactions within the octamer, and the M7 region corresponds to the 'docking domain' that mediates H2A.Z interactions with H3-H4 (Zlatanova and Thakar, 2008).
evidence: This is structural knowledge supported by citation.

claim: The M7 region corresponds to the 'docking domain' that mediates H2A.Z interactions with H3-H4.
source: Structurally the M3 region corresponds to the 'loop 1' that mediates H2A.Z-H2A.Z interactions within the octamer, and the M7 region corresponds to the 'docking domain' that mediates H2A.Z interactions with H3-H4 (Zlatanova and Thakar, 2008).
evidence: This is structural knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Hopping in the proximal dimer region is nucleosome-specific and not observed during unzipping of bare NPS DNA.
source: Hopping in this region is nucleosome-specific, as it is not observed during unzipping of bare NPS DNA (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is an experimental observation comparing nucleosome and bare DNA unzipping.

claim: The reversible nature of hopping transitions contrasts with the irreversible transitions observed deeper in the nucleosome.
source: The reversible nature of this transition contrasts with the irreversible transitions observed deeper in the nucleosome, and may indicate a rapid, small scale unzipping that is not large enough to disrupt the structure of the octamer.
evidence: This is an experimental observation with an interpretation.

claim: WT nucleosomes display an additional peak in the distribution of unzipped bps at approximately 28 bp after the start of the second NPS.
source: Relative to bare DNA, WT nucleosomes display an additional peak in the distribution of unzipped bps, at approximately 28 bp after the start of the second NPS where the most significant contacts between DNA and the H2A-H2B dimer occur (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is an experimental observation from equilibrium hopping data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The 'molecular ruler' consists of eight tandem repeats of an artificially designed 64 bp DNA that has a single well-defined, sequence-encoded pause site when transcribed by Pol II.
source: The 'molecular ruler' consists of eight tandem repeats of an artificially designed 64 bp DNA that has a single well-defined, sequence-encoded pause site when transcribed by Pol II in bulk (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A, dashed rectangle) and in single-molecule assays (Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B–D).
evidence: This describes the experimental design validated by data in Figure 4 and supplements.

claim: The repeating pausing patterns of Pol II within the 'molecular ruler' generated a periodicity of 21.1 ± 0.3 nm.
source: The repeating pausing patterns of Pol II within the 'molecular ruler' generated a periodicity of 21.1 ± 0.3 nm (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B), corresponding to the length of 64 bp DNA under experimental force and buffer conditions.
evidence: This is a quantitative experimental measurement shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: This tethering geometry is superior to prior designs because it isolates Pol II from the beads surfaces, thus mitigating photo-damage.
source: We find this tethering geometry to be superior to prior designs (Hodges et al., 2009; Bintu et al., 2012) because it isolates Pol II from the beads surfaces, thus mitigating photo-damage (Landry et al., 2009).
evidence: This is a methodological claim supported by citation about photo-damage.

claim: Pol II has a median crossing time within the NPS of 11 s for bare NPS DNA.
source: The results show that Pol II has a median crossing time within the NPS of 11 s (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A), a pause free velocity of 28.9 ± 3.0 nt-s−1 (Figure 6—figure supplement 1H), and displays very few backtracking events (0.17 per trace) (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is a quantitative experimental measurement shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Pol II has a pause free velocity of 28.9 ± 3.0 nt-s−1 on bare NPS DNA.
source: The results show that Pol II has a median crossing time within the NPS of 11 s (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A), a pause free velocity of 28.9 ± 3.0 nt-s−1 (Figure 6—figure supplement 1H), and displays very few backtracking events (0.17 per trace) (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is a quantitative experimental measurement shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1H.

claim: Pol II displays very few backtracking events (0.17 per trace) on bare NPS DNA.
source: The results show that Pol II has a median crossing time within the NPS of 11 s (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A), a pause free velocity of 28.9 ± 3.0 nt-s−1 (Figure 6—figure supplement 1H), and displays very few backtracking events (0.17 per trace) (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is a quantitative experimental measurement from Supplementary file 2.

claim: Pol II exhibits a dramatic slow-down with a median crossing time of 129 s for Xenopus WT nucleosomes.
source: As expected, Pol II exhibits a dramatic slow-down, with a median crossing time of 129 s (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B), a pause-free velocity of 11.4 ± 4.1 nt-s−1 (Figure 6—figure supplement 1H), and frequent pausing and backtracking within the NPS region (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is a quantitative experimental measurement shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B.

claim: 59% of Pol II succeeded in crossing the Xenopus WT nucleosome barrier.
source: 59% of Pol II succeeded in crossing the barrier (Figure 6—figure supplement 1F), which is signaled by its reaching the stall site at the end of the template (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is a quantitative experimental measurement shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1F.

claim: The measurements represent a nearly 20-fold resolution and accuracy improvement on previous attempts to obtain a transcriptional map of the nucleosomal barrier.
source: Our measurements represent a nearly 20-fold resolution and accuracy improvement on previous attempts to obtain a transcriptional map of the nucleosomal barrier, since those experiments could only resolve roughly three barrier regions of ~50 bp each, corresponding to entry, central and exit zones (Hodges et al., 2009; Bintu et al., 2012; Fitz et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a comparative claim based on the current data and citations to previous work.

claim: The effect of the barrier begins immediately after the leading edge of Pol II touches the NPS (3 bp peak).
source: First, the effect of the barrier begins immediately after the leading edge of Pol II touches the NPS (3 bp peak); the strength of the barrier is largest at 28 bp and 10–20 bp before the dyad, and is negligible after crossing this pseudo-symmetry axis.
evidence: This is an experimental observation from the transcriptional map in Figure 6A.

claim: The strength of the barrier is largest at 28 bp and 10–20 bp before the dyad.
source: First, the effect of the barrier begins immediately after the leading edge of Pol II touches the NPS (3 bp peak); the strength of the barrier is largest at 28 bp and 10–20 bp before the dyad, and is negligible after crossing this pseudo-symmetry axis.
evidence: This is an experimental observation from the transcriptional map in Figure 6A.

claim: The strength of the barrier is negligible after crossing the dyad.
source: First, the effect of the barrier begins immediately after the leading edge of Pol II touches the NPS (3 bp peak); the strength of the barrier is largest at 28 bp and 10–20 bp before the dyad, and is negligible after crossing this pseudo-symmetry axis.
evidence: This is an experimental observation from the transcriptional map in Figure 6A.

claim: A region between 28–64 bp into the NPS was identified where Pol II enters long-lived pauses and backtracks frequently.
source: Second, we identified a region between 28–64 bp into the NPS where Pol II enters long-lived pauses and backtracks frequently (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is an experimental observation from transcription traces shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The pauses in the 28-64 bp region are consistent among different molecules and exhibit a ~ 10 bp periodicity.
source: These pauses are consistent among different molecules and exhibit a ~ 10 bp periodicity (28, 38, 48, 57, and 64 bp into the NPS).
evidence: This is an experimental observation from multiple transcription traces.

claim: The 28-64 bp region coincides with the region of maximum resistance in the single-molecule unzipping assay.
source: Notably, this region coincides with the region of maximum resistance in the single-molecule unzipping assay (Figures 1E and 2B), implying that the transcriptional barrier encountered by Pol II while crossing the nucleosome reflects, to a first approximation, the barrier mapped by the unzipping assay.
evidence: This is a comparison between two experimental datasets with an interpretation.

claim: Some molecules were permanently arrested in the 28-64 bp region, but those that managed to cross it typically succeeded in reaching the stall site.
source: Third, some molecules were permanently arrested in this region (Figure 5A,B, gray trace), but those that managed to cross it typically succeeded in reaching the stall site shortly thereafter (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is an experimental observation from transcription traces shown in Figure 5.

claim: The 28-64 bp region may play an important regulatory role for barrier crossing by the enzyme.
source: Thus, we speculate that this region (28–64 bp) may play an important regulatory role for barrier crossing by the enzyme.
evidence: This is speculation based on the experimental observations.

claim: The transcriptional map asymmetry is similarly observed in the topographic map, even though the bulkiness of the enzyme does not play a role in those experiments.
source: However, the transcriptional map asymmetry is similarly observed in the topographic map (Figure 1E), even though the bulkiness of the enzyme does not play a role in those experiments.
evidence: This is a comparison between two experimental datasets.

claim: Human nucleosomes confer a significantly higher barrier to transcription than those of Xenopus in the proximal dimer region.
source: As seen in Figure 6A, the maps are quite similar except that human nucleosomes confer a significantly higher barrier to transcription (see Figure 5A–B, Videos 7 and 8 for representative traces) than those of Xenopus in the proximal dimer region (Figure 6A, the 28 bp peak in orange and red panels).
evidence: This is a comparative experimental observation shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Pol II hopping at 28 bp coincides with hopping of the unzipping fork near this region and probably reflects sampling of alternative nucleosomal states ahead of the enzyme.
source: While Pol II hopping at 28 bp coincides with hopping of the unzipping fork near this region and probably reflects sampling of alternative nucleosomal states ahead of the enzyme, hopping at a much deeper location into the nucleosome (63 bp) may have a more complex origin.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on comparing two experimental datasets.

claim: Hopping at 63 bp may be due to local Pol II-histone interactions or re-wrapping of the nucleosome in front of a backtracked enzyme.
source: We hypothesize that these latter dynamics may be due to local Pol II-histone interactions or re-wrapping of the nucleosome in front of a backtracked enzyme.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on experimental observations.

claim: The pause-free velocity of Pol II after exiting the nucleosome resumed to 70% of its value before the crossing.
source: The pause-free velocity of Pol II after exiting the nucleosome resumed to 70% (28.6 ± 0.8 nt-s−1) of its value before the crossing (41.1 ± 1.0 nt-s−1).
evidence: This is a quantitative experimental measurement shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1H.

claim: Rarely (<5%) the pulling curves displayed the force-extension signature normally associated with the presence of a nucleosome after Pol II crossed the barrier.
source: Rarely (<5%) these pulling curves displayed the force-extension signature normally associated with the presence of a nucleosome, suggesting that in situ reassembly of the nucleosome following Pol II traversal was inefficient under our assay conditions.
evidence: This is a quantitative experimental observation with an interpretation.

claim: A similar low efficiency of nucleosome reassembly was observed from transcription assays in bulk in the absence of factors added in trans such as FACT.
source: A similar low efficiency of nucleosome reassembly was observed from transcription assays in bulk in the absence of factors added in trans such as FACT (facilitates chromatin transcription) (Hsieh et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The crossing probabilities of Pol II through H2A.Z and WT nucleosomes are similar (58% and 59%, respectively).
source: While the crossing probabilities of Pol II through H2A.Z and WT nucleosomes are similar (58% and 59%, respectively) (Figure 6—figure supplement 1F), the distributions of pause sites within the NPS are markedly different (Figure 6A) in that H2A.Z is seen to cause a global redistribution of Pol II pause sites along the entire NPS.
evidence: This is a quantitative experimental measurement shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1F.

claim: H2A.Z causes a global redistribution of Pol II pause sites along the entire NPS.
source: While the crossing probabilities of Pol II through H2A.Z and WT nucleosomes are similar (58% and 59%, respectively) (Figure 6—figure supplement 1F), the distributions of pause sites within the NPS are markedly different (Figure 6A) in that H2A.Z is seen to cause a global redistribution of Pol II pause sites along the entire NPS.
evidence: This is an experimental observation from the transcriptional map in Figure 6A.

claim: The scattered distribution of pause sites in H2A.Z nucleosomes differs significantly from that of WT nucleosome where most pauses occur before the dyad.
source: Such scattered distribution (3, 28, 36, 59, 66, 87, 101, 115, 125 and 138 bp) differs significantly from that of WT nucleosome (3, 28, 57, 64 bp) where most pauses occur before the dyad.
evidence: This is a comparative experimental observation from Figure 6A.

claim: The first pause site at ~3 bp is observed in every molecular trajectory obtained with H2A.Z nucleosomes.
source: Furthermore, these differences are unlikely to stem from H2A.Z nucleosomes being mis-positioned on the starting template, because the first pause site at ~3 bp, where the leading edge of Pol II begins to interact with the nucleosome, is observed in every molecular trajectory obtained with H2A.Z nucleosomes.
evidence: This is an experimental observation that rules out an alternative explanation.

claim: Pol II transcription through human uH2B nucleosomes has a slightly higher passage probability (76%) than through hWT nucleosomes.

evidence: This is a quantitative experimental observation from Figure 6A with an interpretation.

claim: The overall pause-free velocities of Pol II transcription through H2A.Z (11.4 ± 7.1 nt-s−1) and uH2B nucleosomes (12.9 ± 3.4 nt-s−1) are lower than that through hWT (18.2 ± 7.1 nt-s−1) nucleosomes.
source: The overall pause-free velocities of Pol II transcription through H2A.Z (11.4 ± 7.1 nt-s−1) and uH2B nucleosomes (12.9 ± 3.4 nt-s−1) are lower than that through hWT (18.2 ± 7.1 nt-s−1) nucleosomes (Figure 6—figure supplement 1H).

claim: The median crossing times of Pol II through H2A.Z (262 s) and uH2B (304 s) nucleosomes are longer than that through hWT nucleosomes (230 s).
source: Consequently, the median crossing times of Pol II through H2A.Z (262 s) and uH2B (304 s) nucleosomes are longer than that through hWT nucleosomes (230 s) (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C–E).

claim: Pol II takes longer to cross uH2B or H2A.Z than hWT nucleosomes when including pausing, translocation and backtracking.
source: Including pausing, translocation and backtracking, Pol II takes longer to cross uH2B or H2A.Z than hWT nucleosomes (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is shown in the crossing time distributions in Figure 6B.

claim: Backtrack durations are longer when Pol II transcribes through H2A.Z nucleosomes than through WT and uH2B counterparts.
source: The average number of backtracks and backtrack depths are similar, but backtrack durations are longer when Pol II transcribes through H2A.Z nucleosomes than through WT and uH2B counterparts (Supplementary file 2), which may again reflect the broader extent of histone-DNA interactions in H2A.Z nucleosomes.
evidence: This is a quantitative experimental measurement from Supplementary file 2 with an interpretation.

claim: Arrest positions were more scattered for Pol II transcribing through uH2B and H2A.Z than through WT nucleosomes.
source: Failure to recover from some backtracks seems to contribute to Pol II arrests, the positions of which were more scattered for Pol II transcribing through uH2B and H2A.Z than through WT nucleosomes (Figure 6—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: This is an experimental observation shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1G.

claim: H2A.Z mainly enhances the width and uH2B mainly enhances the height of nucleosomal barrier to transcription.
source: Collectively, these data reveal that H2A.Z mainly enhances the width and uH2B mainly enhances the height of nucleosomal barrier to transcription.
evidence: This is a summary interpretation of multiple experimental observations.

claim: uH2B nucleosomes pose an overall higher barrier magnitude than their WT counterparts to the passage of polymerase, consistent with previously reported higher stability.
source: Consistent with the previously reported higher stability of uH2B nucleosomes (Batta et al., 2011; Chandrasekharan et al., 2009), they pose an overall higher barrier magnitude––especially in the region near the dyad––than their WT counterparts to the passage of polymerase.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the current data supported by citations to previous work.

claim: For WT and H2A.Z, but not for uH2B nucleosomes, the transcriptional map replicates the corresponding topography map.
source: It is also worth noting that for WT and H2A.Z, but not for uH2B nucleosomes, the transcriptional map replicates the corresponding topography map, suggesting that there could be uH2B-Pol II specific interactions that are not present in the unzipping assay.
evidence: This is a comparative observation with an interpretation.

claim: H2A.Z or uH2B by themselves affect the crossing dynamics of Pol II.
source: Our findings provide direct evidence that H2A.Z or uH2B by themselves affect the crossing dynamics of Pol II; and despite their differential effects on nucleosome topography, they both represent stronger barriers than WT nucleosomes for Pol II.
evidence: This is a summary of the experimental findings.

claim: Despite their differential effects on nucleosome topography, H2A.Z and uH2B both represent stronger barriers than WT nucleosomes for Pol II.
source: Our findings provide direct evidence that H2A.Z or uH2B by themselves affect the crossing dynamics of Pol II; and despite their differential effects on nucleosome topography, they both represent stronger barriers than WT nucleosomes for Pol II.
evidence: This is a summary of the experimental findings.

claim: The enzyme behaves as a ratchet that makes progress by rectifying the unwrapping fluctuations of the nucleosomal DNA.

evidence: This is an interpretation from the mechanical model shown in Figure 7D,E.

claim: The proximal dimer region of the nucleosome (~28 bp) in the transcription direction is a major physical barrier for Pol II.
source: Our results reveal that the proximal dimer region of the nucleosome (~28 bp) in the transcription direction is a major physical barrier for Pol II and may serve as an important regulatory checkpoint for gene expression.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data.

claim: The proximal dimer region may serve as an important regulatory checkpoint for gene expression.
source: Our results reveal that the proximal dimer region of the nucleosome (~28 bp) in the transcription direction is a major physical barrier for Pol II and may serve as an important regulatory checkpoint for gene expression.
evidence: This is speculation based on the experimental data.

claim: Pausing at the SHL(-5) location is accompanied by extensive hopping dynamics, likely reflecting unwrapping/rewrapping of the nucleosomal DNA around the octamer and/or structural rearrangements of the nucleosome.
source: Interestingly, pausing at this location is accompanied by extensive hopping dynamics, likely reflecting unwrapping/rewrapping of the nucleosomal DNA around the octamer and/or structural rearrangements of the nucleosome.
evidence: This is an experimental observation with an interpretation.

claim: Partially unwrapped nucleosomal intermediates have been detected in vitro by time-resolved small angle X-ray scattering, by cryo-EM and in vivo by MNase-seq.
source: Indeed, partially unwrapped nucleosomal intermediates have been detected in vitro by time-resolved small angle X-ray scattering (Chen et al., 2014), by cryo-EM (Bilokapic et al., 2018) and in vivo by MNase-seq (Ramachandran et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The location of partially unwrapped nucleosomal intermediates coincides with the different nucleosomal hopping states observed as the unzipping fork reaches the proximal dimer.
source: The location of these structural intermediates coincides with the different nucleosomal hopping states observed as the unzipping fork reaches the proximal dimer, reinforcing the interpretation that local DNA/histone interactions determine the dynamics of Pol II in this region and its ultimate progress beyond it.
evidence: This is an interpretation connecting the current data with previous structural observations.

claim: The proximal dimer region and not the dyad represents the highest barrier to an elongating Pol II.
source: Unambiguously assigning Pol II's residence time with bp resolution has allowed us to define a transcriptional map of the barrier, which indicates that the proximal dimer region and not the dyad represents the highest barrier to an elongating Pol II.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the high-resolution transcriptional map data.

claim: The change in dynamics of the polymerase in the proximal dimer region provides a crucial time window to allow for other facilitative or inhibitory factors to bind.
source: We posit here that the change in dynamics of the polymerase, progressing slowly in this region, provides a crucial time window to allow for other facilitative or inhibitory factors to bind and further modulate the strength of the barrier to the transcribing enzyme.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the experimental observations.

claim: FACT may bind to the nucleosome and remove one histone dimer ahead of the Pol II and reassemble the nucleosome after Pol II traversal.
source: For instance, FACT may bind to the nucleosome and remove one histone dimer ahead of the Pol II and reassemble the nucleosome after Pol II traversal (Belotserkovskaya et al., 2003; Mason and Struhl, 2003; Chen et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work on FACT function.

claim: H2A.Z and uH2B mainly affect the proximal dimer region, although their effects are not circumscribed to this location.
source: Consistent with these observations, modifications that play important regulatory roles such as H2A.Z and uH2B, mainly affect the proximal dimer region, although their effects are not circumscribed to this location.
evidence: This is a summary of the experimental observations.

claim: The topographic map of the WT and H2A.Z barriers before the dyad closely parallels the transcriptional map of Pol II.
source: Significantly, the topographic map of the WT and H2A.Z barriers before the dyad, as determined here by force-induced nucleosomal DNA unwinding, closely parallels the transcriptional map of Pol II, indicating that to a first approximation, the ability of the enzyme to cross the barriers in this region is dictated by the energetic requirements of disrupting DNA-histone interactions.
evidence: This is a comparative observation with an interpretation.

claim: In vitro, H2A.Z has been observed to either enhance or decrease nucleosome stability depending on the assays used.
source: In vitro, H2A.Z has been observed to either enhance or decrease nucleosome stability depending on the assays used (Zlatanova and Thakar, 2008; Bönisch and Hake, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: H2A.Z redistributes the strength of the barrier across and beyond the dyad, effectively increasing its width.
source: Our improved optical tweezers experiments offer unprecedented resolution that captures a more complex picture in which H2A.Z redistributes the strength of the barrier across and beyond the dyad, effectively increasing its width.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the high-resolution experimental data.

claim: The physical barriers across the H2A.Z nucleosome are lower, yet more globally distributed.
source: Accordingly, the physical barriers across the H2A.Z nucleosome are lower, yet more globally distributed.
evidence: This is a summary of the experimental observations.

claim: The effect of H2A.Z on the nucleosomal barrier can be seen as that of re-distributing the strength of the barrier from height to width.
source: The effect of H2A.Z on the nucleosomal barrier can be seen as that of re-distributing the strength of the barrier from height to width.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental data.

claim: By dividing the height of the barrier into several smaller ones, H2A.Z nucleosomes provide the enzyme more opportunities at different locations to pause, backtrack and possibly interact with regulatory factors.
source: By dividing the height of the barrier into several smaller ones, H2A.Z nucleosomes provides the enzyme more opportunities at different locations to pause, backtrack and possibly interact with regulatory factors acting in trans such as chaperones and chromatin remodelers.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental data.

claim: The strong barrier posed by H2A.Z nucleosomes may explain its role in poising quiescent genes for activation in yeast.
source: The strong barrier posed by H2A.Z nucleosomes may explain its role in poising quiescent genes for activation in yeast (Santisteban et al., 2011) and its prevalence in +1 nucleosomes across eukaryotic genomes (Weber et al., 2014).
evidence: This is an interpretation connecting the current data with previous in vivo observations.

claim: The observation that H2A.Z facilitates transcription in multi-cellular organisms is more likely due to recruitment of trans-acting factors.
source: In contrast, the observation that H2A.Z facilitates transcription in multi-cellular organisms (Weber et al., 2014) is more likely due to recruitment of trans-acting factors.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the current data and cited literature.

claim: uH2B strengthens histone-DNA interactions at the dimer region and increases the overall barrier strength to Pol II.
source: Using homogeneous, chemically-defined recombinant nucleosomes, we also demonstrated that uH2B strengthens histone-DNA interactions at the dimer region and increases the overall barrier strength to Pol II.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data.

claim: While uH2B occurs at the dimer region, its effect on Pol II transcription propagates to other regions of the nucleosome including the region preceding the dyad.
source: Interestingly, while uH2B occurs at the dimer region, its effect on Pol II transcription propagates to other regions of the nucleosome including the region preceding the dyad.
evidence: This is an experimental observation.

claim: In vivo, H2B ubiquitination is highly dynamic and both the addition and removal of ubiquitin are required for optimal transcription.
source: In vivo, H2B ubiquitination is highly dynamic and both the addition and removal of ubiquitin are required for optimal transcription (Wyce et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Higher levels of H2A.Z and uH2B are observed in transcriptionally silent gene promoters in yeast.
source: Nevertheless, higher levels of H2A.Z and uH2B are observed in transcriptionally silent gene promoters in yeast (Batta et al., 2011; Zhang et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous genomic studies.

claim: Preventing H2B ubiquitination in yeast led to increased Pol II occupancy and transcription from quiescent promoters.
source: Preventing H2B ubiquitination in yeast led to increased Pol II occupancy and transcription from quiescent promoters (Batta et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: H2A.Z and uH2B provide orthogonal and selective means to enhance the transcription barrier thus contributing to the maintenance of the transcriptional ground state and to gene silencing.
source: These observations are consistent with our data that H2A.Z and uH2B provide orthogonal and selective means to enhance the transcription barrier thus contributing to the maintenance of the transcriptional ground state and to gene silencing.
evidence: This is an interpretation connecting the current data with previous in vivo observations.

claim: While H2A.Z and uH2B modifications may act indirectly through their actions on the binding of trans-acting factors, they exert a direct and significant effect on transcription dynamics by Pol II.
source: Our results show that while these modifications may also act indirectly through their actions on the binding of trans-acting factors, they exert a direct and significant effect on transcription dynamics by Pol II.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data.

claim: The mechanical model is quite general and should prove useful in predicting the behavior of Pol II through alternative barriers.
source: This model is quite general and should prove useful in predicting the behavior of Pol II through alternative barriers, and in understanding the mechanics of barrier crossing for other molecular motors.
evidence: This is a claim about the utility of the model.

claim: The dynamics of Pol II transcription through the nucleosome in vivo are affected by numerous other factors such as higher-order chromatin folding, DNA topology, and transcription regulators.
source: The dynamics of Pol II transcription through the nucleosome in vivo are affected by numerous other factors such as higher-order chromatin folding, DNA topology, and transcription regulators including histone chaperones, elongation factors, and chromatin remodelers.
evidence: This is established knowledge about in vivo transcription.

claim: Epigenetic modifications are potent regulators of eukaryotic gene expression.
source: Because epigenetic modifications are potent regulators of eukaryotic gene expression, these results shed new light on the mechanistic link between modifications enriched on the +1 nucleosome and the barrier to transcription.
evidence: This is established knowledge.

claim: The real-time characterization of the dynamics of Pol II molecules traversing through nucleosomes at the highest resolution and accuracy reported so far constitutes important steps towards uncovering the physical mechanisms underpinning the regulation of eukaryotic gene expression.
source: More broadly, the real-time characterization of the dynamics of Pol II molecules traversing through nucleosomes at the highest resolution and accuracy reported so far, and the resulting nucleosome transcriptional map, constitute important steps towards uncovering the physical mechanisms underpinning the regulation of eukaryotic gene expression.
